title: Risk, response, and the first stage
dek: Capacity revealed under pressure across climate adaptation, emergency response, and nonlinear instruments.
trend: This issue’s common thread is capacity revealed under pressure. Higher cyclone risk appears to induce adaptation; rural EMS gaps persist even where income differences do not; and a flexible first stage can reveal instrument strength that a linear model masks. Across all three, measured exposure is not the mechanism itself: institutions, service placement, and functional-form choices determine how exposure becomes an outcome.

articles.summary: The authors estimate each country’s evolving disaster-arrival rate, then interact that risk with cyclone strikes in a 48-country panel from 1980–2019. Cyclones reduce per-capita growth by about one percentage point in a typical country-year, but the damage is smaller when current risk is elevated; the estimated offset is roughly 9% at a one-standard-deviation rise in risk. The interpretation is clever, though it relies on smooth risk trends not proxying for other country-specific changes.

paper.title: The Return to Adaptation in a Changing Climate
paper.authors: Harrison Hong; Serena Ng; Jiangmin Xu
paper.abstract: This paper estimates whether economies adapt as extreme-weather arrival rates rise. Using tropical cyclones across 48 countries, it tests whether damage per disaster declines when risk rises above historical baselines and quantifies the welfare value of adaptation.

articles.summary: Town-level Connecticut data show rural mean EMS response time near 13 minutes—roughly twice the non-rural mean—while median household income does not explain variation within either group. Geography, stationing, staffing, and volunteer-service capacity look more plausible than town income alone. The evidence is descriptive rather than causal and uses 2016 data.

paper.title: Socioeconomic factors influencing rural-urban ambulance response time disparities in Connecticut
paper.abstract: Abstract Across the U.S, it is a documented fact that rural areas have longer ambulance response times and tend to have lower median income. The objective of this study was to test if the rural-urban emergency medical service (EMS) response time disparity was related to wealth disparity in the state of Connecticut. All mean EMS response times were sourced from the 2016 Office of Emergency Medical Services Data Report. Rural definitions were sourced from the Connecticut Office of Rural Health. Median income data was drawn from the Connecticut Office of Policy and Management. A Mann-Whitney U test determined if the average rural EMS response time was greater than the non-rural EMS response time. Pearson coefficients quantified the relationship between median income and EMS response time. A t-test ascertained if the average median income differed between the two datasets. The mean EMS response time was 12.98 min (SD = 3.36) rural and 8.26 min (SD = 2.12) non-rural. Rural mean response time and median income were not significantly correlated ( r = -.148, p =.247); non-rural mean response time and median income were also not significantly related. No significant disparity was detected (t=0.478, p =.633) between the mean rural household income ($98,258) and mean non-rural household income ($95,706). Significant disparities in EMS response times can exist between rural and non-rural towns separate from median income trends, as is the case in Connecticut. These findings may have limited generalizability because of Connecticut’s relatively high median income as compared to other states yet may be relevant to states with similar economic metrics.

articles.summary: A linear first stage can hide a strong but nonlinear relationship between an instrument and endogenous regressor. The proposed cross-fitted Super Learner control-function estimator performs well in nonlinear simulations and is illustrated with wind direction as an instrument for air pollution. It repairs misspecification-induced weakness; it cannot create identification when the instrument is genuinely weak.

paper.title: Weak Instrumental Variables Due to Nonlinearities in Panel Data: A Super Learner Control Function Estimator
paper.abstract: The paper shows how an incorrectly linear reduced form can make instruments appear weak in panel data and proposes a flexible Super Learner control-function estimator.
